symptoms: Small rectangular lesions with parallel edges bounded by leaf veins
Initially tan or yellow spots turning grayish brown with age
Lesions may coalesce to form large blighted areas on leaves, especially starting from lower canopy
management: Remove or bury heavily infected crop residue where practical and conservation tillage allows.
Adopt crop rotation with non-host crops (legumes such as beans, cowpeas, or sunflower) for at least 1-2 seasons.
Consult a local Kenyan extension officer before considering PCPB-registered fungicides (never spray uncertified products).
prevention: Plant certified KALRO or KEPHIS approved resistant or tolerant maize hybrids (e.g., modern mid-altitude varieties).
Avoid continuous monocropping of maize on the same parcel.
Ensure balanced plant nutrition—excess nitrogen combined with potassium deficiency elevates susceptibility.
monitoring: Scout lower and middle leaves weekly starting at knee-high (V6-V8) through silking (R1).
Track upward lesion spread toward the ear leaf; disease reaching ear leaf before grain filling causes major yield loss.
escalation: Lesions reach ear leaf or above during silking/tasseling stage.
Over 30% of field foliage displays coalescing lesions.
Persistent warm, overcast, and high-humidity weather forecasted in highland maize zones.
kenya_notes: Significant in wet, humid highland and mid-altitude maize basins including Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu, Kakamega, and Kericho. Continuous maize farming and minimum tillage with infected stover heighten local risk.
